answer.sourceLine: This one is genuine. Horton the Elephant says it in Horton Hears a Who!, published by Random House in 1954 — Wikiquote’s sourced section files the line there, and a review in the December 1954 Dartmouth Alumni Magazine was already quoting it as the book’s moral within months of publication.

source.excerpt: A person’s a person, no matter how small.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section for Dr. Seuss ↗ lists the line under Horton Hears a Who! (1954), both on its own and inside Horton’s longer ‘Don’t give up! I believe in you all’ speech to the Whos.
Contemporaneous confirmation: a review by Maude D. French in the December 1954 Dartmouth Alumni Magazine ↗ quotes the line verbatim as the book’s lesson, and names Random House as publisher at $2.50.
The book itself is catalogued and scanned: the Internet Archive’s copy ↗ records Random House, New York, 1954 (lending-restricted, from the Boston Public Library).
Background on the book — the Japan visit behind the theme, the dedication to a Japanese friend, and the line’s later political career — is set out on Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗.
source.excerptNote: Horton shouts it while urging the Whos to make themselves heard; Wikiquote records the fuller declaration it sits inside. We quote only the sentence here — the book is still in copyright, and the point of this page is the attribution, not the text.

source.rightsNote: Horton Hears a Who! was first published in 1954, well after the 1930 US public-domain cutoff, so both the text and the illustrations remain under copyright. Wikipedia lists Random House as publisher, and NPR identifies Karl ZoBell as an attorney acting for Dr. Seuss Enterprises and for Geisel’s widow Audrey — the estate actively polices how the line is reused. Quoting the sentence with attribution is ordinary citation; reproducing the book’s pages or artwork is not.

author.name: Dr. Seuss
author.heading: About Dr. Seuss
author.metaLine: 1904–1991 · American children’s author, illustrator and political cartoonist
author.bio: Theodor Seuss Geisel was born in Springfield, Massachusetts on 2 March 1904 and died in San Diego on 24 September 1991. Before the picture books made him a household name he worked as an illustrator, animator and political cartoonist — a background that shows in how bluntly moral his children’s stories can be. Horton Hears a Who! (1954) is the clearest case: Geisel framed its central theme as his reaction to a visit to Japan, and dedicated the book to a Japanese friend.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is solid — this really is Dr. Seuss. What travels badly is where people think it came from, how they word it, and what they attach to it.

items.why: Horton and the Narrator both say the line in the Blue Sky/20th Century Fox adaptation, per Wikiquote’s page for the film ↗, so a lot of people date the quote to 2008. It is fifty-four years older than that: the book was published by Random House in 1954, and the line was already being quoted in a review that December ↗.

items.who: ‘A person is a person, no matter how small’
items.why: The contraction is not decorative — it is what makes the line scan in Seuss’s meter. The flattened version circulates widely, including in NPR’s 2008 report ↗, where a Colorado campaigner quotes it as ‘A person is a person no matter how small’. Seuss wrote ‘A person’s a person’.

Wikipedia records that the book has been adopted by the US anti-abortion movement since the 1980s, and that the reading was criticised by Audrey Geisel and by Karl ZoBell of Dr. Seuss Enterprises. ZoBell told NPR ↗ that she disliked people hijacking Dr. Seuss characters to front their own points of view, and that the Geisels never wanted the characters used for any political purpose. The quote is real; the politics were bolted on afterwards.

items.who: ‘…and the smallest among you’s the greatest of all’
items.why: This continuation is frequently appended in social-media graphics, but it is not part of the sentence Wikiquote sources to the book, and it does not appear on Wikiquote’s page for the 2008 film ↗ either. Treat the eight-word sentence as the quote; treat anything welded onto the end of it as unsourced until someone shows you the page.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Seuss’s, written for Horton Hears a Who! and published by Random House in 1954 — Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ puts it there, and a reviewer was already repeating it in December of that year.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Wikipedia records that the book’s main theme — a person’s a person no matter how small — was Geisel’s reaction to his visit to Japan, where he saw the importance of the individual emerging as a concept, and that he used the story as an allegory for the American post-war occupation. He dedicated the book to a Japanese friend. So the most quotable sentence in American children’s literature started life as a note about how an occupying power should treat the people it occupies.

2008 was the year that history got complicated. Wikipedia notes that since the 1980s the book has been adopted by the United States anti-abortion movement, some reading the line as an allegory for the fetus — an interpretation criticised by Geisel’s widow Audrey and by Karl ZoBell, an attorney for Dr. Seuss Enterprises. NPR reported from the Los Angeles premiere of the animated film that year, where activists handed out flyers made to look like movie tickets; ZoBell, who had represented Seuss’s interests for some forty years, told NPR that Audrey Geisel disliked people hijacking Dr. Seuss characters or material to front their own points of view, and that the Geisels never wanted the characters used for any political purpose.
context.detailsSummary: Real Seuss, in a sea of fake Seuss
detailsBody: Dr. Seuss is one of the internet’s busiest quote magnets, which is why this one deserves the contrast. Wikiquote’s own Misattributed section for Seuss reassigns ‘Sometimes you will never know the value of a moment until it becomes a memory’ to Georges Duhamel, ‘Those who mind don’t matter, and those who matter don’t mind’ to Bernard Baruch, and the ‘we’re all a little weird’ passage to Robert Fulghum; its Disputed section flags ‘Don’t cry because it’s over. Smile because it happened’ as attributed to Seuss without citation.
‘A person’s a person, no matter how small’ is the opposite case: a line so firmly documented in a specific 1954 book that a contemporaneous reviewer was already repeating it as the book’s point.
